analysis.one_liner: Bans new federal leases for offshore oil and gas drilling and onshore coal, oil, and gas extraction.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have ended new oil, gas, and coal leasing on federal land and waters, was introduced with 25 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the Interior Department from issuing, renewing, or extending leases for oil, gas, tar sands, oil shale, and coal on federal land and in all federal offshore waters, including the Gulf of Mexico, the Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic oceans. It would also cancel existing offshore leases in three Alaskan waters within 60 days, with narrow exceptions for national security threats and pre-existing contracts. The stated goal is to keep roughly 90 percent of the potential emissions from federally owned fossil fuels in the ground [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to air pollution and climate damage: the bill's findings say ending new federal leases would prevent about 90 percent of the potential emissions from federal fossil fuels, limiting droughts, wildfires, rising seas, and ocean acidification described in its findings [S3]. Coastal communities, fisheries, and taxpayers who bear disaster and cleanup costs also benefit; the federal government currently sells these publicly owned resources to private companies at below-full value.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone exposed to fossil fuel pollution and climate risk

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management from issuing, renewing, reinstating, or extending any nonproducing lease or any exploration or production authorization for fossil fuels in the Arctic, Atlantic, and Pacific oceans, the Gulf of Mexico, and all other outer Continental Shelf areas [S2] [S3].
Requires cancellation within 60 days of existing offshore leases in the Beaufort Sea, Cook Inlet, and Chukchi Sea off Alaska [S2] [S3].

Bars the Bureau of Land Management from holding lease sales or issuing, renewing, reinstating, or extending nonproducing leases for onshore coal, oil, tar sands, oil shale, and gas on federal land under the Mineral Leasing Act [S2] [S3].

Contains exceptions only for leases needed to address an imminent national security threat, and for renewing or extending pre-existing contracts when blocking them would likely cause a court to find a material breach [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies that depend on access to federally owned minerals would lose future lease sales and, offshore Alaska, existing leases. Federal and state budgets would lose some royalty revenue, and workers and towns in fossil-fuel-producing regions, particularly coal communities, would face continued economic transition pressure. Consumers could see modest upward pressure on energy prices as new federal supply shrinks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, gas, and coal companies using federal land

drawbacks.text: Blocking new federal leases would reduce future royalty revenue flowing to the Treasury and to states that share in federal mineral revenues, and would shrink the supply of federally owned coal, oil, and gas available to energy markets, with possible price effects for consumers [S3].

Fossil fuel extraction supports jobs and tax bases in producing regions, particularly coal communities; cutting off new federal leases accelerates economic losses in those towns, and the bill contains no transition assistance for affected workers [S3].

A unilateral end to US federal leasing would not by itself stop global emissions if other producers filled the gap, meaning some of the climate benefit could be offset by shifted production, while the domestic costs would fall directly on US producers and communities [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits are large but long-term and widely shared: less climate damage and pollution from publicly owned fuels, with the bill's own findings citing a 2-degree-Celsius warming threshold and a need to leave most proven fossil reserves unburned [S3]. The costs are concentrated and real: lost royalties, lost jobs in coal and oil regions, and possible energy price pressure, with no worker transition aid included in the bill. Whether the trade is worth it depends on how much one weighs near-term energy supply and producing-region jobs against long-term climate damage; the bill as written asks producing regions and companies to absorb the cost for a broadly shared benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote for the rest of the Congress [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Representative Jared Huffman and nine original cosponsors introduced the bill on April 28, 2017, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day [S1] [S5].

On May 11, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources; the action history shows no further action, hearing, markup, or vote through the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019 [S5].

All 25 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill was introduced in the first weeks of a Congress in which Republicans controlled the House, the committee, and the White House [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal companies kept access to new federal lease sales and existing Alaskan offshore leases, since no restriction was ever enacted; energy-producing regions also avoided the transition the bill would have accelerated. The 25 cosponsors' constituents gained nothing, as the bill died without even a hearing [S4] [S5].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies and their lease access

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported the bill; with Republicans holding the House majority, the bill never advanced past committee referral [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Would lose the ability to obtain new leases and exploration authorizations in the Gulf of Mexico, Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic waters, and would lose existing leases off Alaska [S3]. These companies profit from extracting publicly owned oil and gas, and the climate and pollution costs of that extraction fall on the public.

Would be cut off from new federal coal leases on public land, the main source of US coal production. Coal combustion is a leading source of the greenhouse gases and air pollution the bill's findings describe [S3].

industries.industry: Onshore oil, gas, tar sands, and oil shale producers
industries.note: Would lose new lease sales and lease renewals on federal land under the Mineral Leasing Act, shrinking future access to publicly owned minerals [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: State and local governments in energy-producing regions
industries.note: Would lose a share of federal mineral royalty revenue tied to new leasing, alongside their residents' exposure to the extraction economy's decline; the bill offered no replacement revenue or transition aid [S3].
